newsitem.title: USA: Landmark Florida tobacco lawsuit ready for trial.
newsitem.headline: Landmark Florida tobacco lawsuit ready for trial.

text.p: Florida's billion-dollar lawsuit against tobacco companies to recover the cost of treating sick smokers could strike a fundamental blow to the industry and change the way U.S. companies do business, experts said.
Jury selection was scheduled to begin Friday in a 1995 lawsuit brought by the state against major cigarette makers.
It aims to force them to repay the costs for Medicaid treatment of thousands of Floridians allegedly harmed by tobacco smoke.
As the first of 40 similar state lawsuits brought against the industry to go to trial, the case is being carefully watched by legal scholars and financial markets.

But with a $368.5 billion global settlement under discussion in Washington, there is a chance that the lawsuit will not be resolved in court. Congress may approve the global pact, rendering the lawsuit moot, or Florida could settle, as did Mississippi.
Yet the fact that Florida's lawsuit has reached trial makes the case a potential watershed in the legal war on tobacco.
"Florida is ground zero in the battle," said Tim Howard, a private lawyer coordinating the state's case.
Like many past lawsuits against the industry, Florida's lawsuit claims tobacco companies made a dangerous and defective product and misled the public about its risks.

But the lawsuit differs dramatically in one respect. Where past actions were brought by smokers or family members who said they were directly hurt by cigarettes, Florida is a third party, unaffected by smoke and seeking only to recover costs.
In the past, the industry offered a standard defence: that smokers knew the risk of smoking and chose to take it.
"Here they can't blame the state because the state didn't smoke," Howard said.

The case promises to break new legal ground if it succeeds in forcing the industry to pay a claim by a third party rather than a smoker, said Christopher Mueller, a professor of complex litigation at the University of Colorado.

The lawsuit is predicated on 1994 amendments to the state's Medicaid Third Party Liability Act -- legislation that specifically targeted the cigarette industry. That law makes Florida's attempt to recoup Medicaid losses unique.
Without it, lawyers would have to advance new common-law legal theories in order to argue that tobacco companies should compensate an entity, the state, that was not directly harmed.

"I think that if Florida prevails and collects Medicaid damages, it will establish the principle that cigarette makers are liable for the medical damage that their product imposes on society," Mueller said. "This will be a bellwether case."
In pretrial rulings, Palm Beach Circuit Judge Harold Cohen stripped tobacco of some planned defences, including the claim that Medicaid patients knew the dangers of smoking.
Richard Daynard, a Northeastern University law professor and chairman of the anti-smoking Tobacco Products Liability Project, said Cohen's rulings have strengthened the state's case.
"The state still has to prove these guys lied, cheated and stole," he said. "But I think the judge has been tough-minded. He's leaving the state with a bulletproof case."
In his rulings, Cohen wiped out $16 billion in future claims the state had intended to make, leaving Florida to pursue about $1 billion for damages sustained after the 1994 law took effect.

But he also allowed Florida to advance the theory that cigarette makers violated racketeering laws, thus raising tobacco's potential bill by allowing the state to lay claim to billions of dollars in past industry profits.
"That could be more money than anybody has yet talked about," Daynard said. "The industry clearly makes many billions of dollars in profits every year."

Howard said the ultimate impact of a Florida victory could be to force U.S. companies to be more responsible for their products. "It potentially changes the whole structure of how American business is run," he said.

Stephen Krigbaum, an attorney for Philip Morris Cos. Inc., said the defence has assembled as many as 200 witnesses for trial. "We have made some serious inroads into the state's charges and we are ready to pursue the matter further," he said.

The Medicaid trial, coupled with an ongoing Miami trial in which flight attendants are suing for damages caused by secondhand smoke, could produce some volatility in tobacco stocks in the short term, analysts said.
But a resolution, by way of congressional approval of the global pact, a Florida settlement or a verdict will bolster stocks, Smith Barney tobacco analyst Martin Feldman said.
"The market prefers the defined quantum of a settlement to the uncertainty of a litigation threat," he said.

Cohen will begin jury selection Friday with a pool of 300 from which six jurors and nine alternates will be selected. The process is expected to take four or five weeks, with testimony beginning in early September.
